title: Kganyago on how public scrutiny sustains central bank independence
summary: Lesetja Kganyago used his acceptance speech at the Sunday Times Top 100 Companies Awards in Johannesburg on 12 November to explain why the South African Reserve Bank depends on a credible press. For the governor, public confidence helps the Bank fulfil its mandate. Two commitments are within its own control: explaining its conduct and acting consistently with that mandate. Both take time to establish a reputation. A newspaper contributes something the Bank cannot provide for itself when its journalists independently assess whether it has delivered (pp. 1–2).

Kganyago traced the problem back to his previous Sunday Times award in 2017. In his account, attacks on mainstream media in the United States spread internationally and encouraged hostility and misinformation. The pandemic subsequently put further pressure on the news organisations people relied upon. South Africa also had domestic reasons for mistrust. State capture had weakened public institutions, impaired service delivery and aggravated the economic crisis. Public anger could then reach institutions that had retained their independence. His argument distinguishes what a particular institution does from the reputation it inherits by association with other parts of the state (pp. 1–2).

The example he chose was an early procedural decision by Tito Mboweni. When establishing the Monetary Policy Committee, Mboweni invited the media to the opening of its inaugural meeting. Citizens whose lives were affected by monetary decisions could gain insight into how the committee reached them. This was a particular invitation to the start of one meeting. The address gives no account of how much the public subsequently understood, or which forms of reporting changed opinion. It does establish why access mattered to the former governor and why his successor connected it to accountability (p. 2).

Kganyago closed by sharing credit with colleagues, the people the Bank serves and the institutions that scrutinise it. The address sets out his view of independence as a public relationship and contains no interest rate decision or new economic forecast (pp. 2–3).

questions.question: Does explaining a decision change understanding before it changes trust?
questions.detail: Kganyago assigns the press two jobs: explaining the stance and assessing delivery. Compare what readers can recall about a decision, its rationale and its consequences with what they report about confidence in the MPC. A reader can accurately describe the committee’s choice and still disagree with it. Separate measures would show which outcome clearer reporting can reasonably influence.

questions.question: How much of the Reserve Bank’s reputation is shared with other public institutions?
questions.detail: The speech suggests that dissatisfaction following state capture reached institutions with different records of independence. A survey could separately ask about the Bank, other public bodies, perceived service delivery and recognition of the Bank’s remit. Repeated observations around events outside monetary policy would help distinguish common shifts in sentiment from responses specifically to an MPC decision.

questions.question: Which kinds of access allow independent scrutiny of the committee’s reasoning?
questions.detail: Mboweni opened the beginning of an inaugural meeting. That example leaves open what journalists could verify about later decisions. Compare the questions raised in coverage with the decision rationale publicly available at the time, and examine whether follow-up explanations resolved identifiable uncertainties. Access, comprehension and the freedom to criticise are different outcomes, each relevant to the governor’s account of accountability.

limitation: A short acceptance address provides a historical example and the governor’s institutional argument. It includes no survey, chart or estimate of the effect of press access on public confidence.
